final_proof:
The statement needs the usual hypotheses on differential operators, and its two parts have different answers. The assertion about equations is true (under those hypotheses), but the proposed induction does not prove it. The analogous assertion about linear inequations is false.

Let K be a differential field with derivation δ, let K[D] be the ring of linear ordinary differential operators, with Da=aD+δ(a), and let the operators act on a differential field extension E of K. Suppose L_j ∈ K[D] and f_j ∈ E. We first prove the precise equation statement

    ⋀_{j=1}^n (L_j x=f_j)  ⇔  (Lx=f) ∧ ψ,

where ψ contains neither x nor any derivative of x.

Assume first that at least one L_j is nonzero. Consider the left ideal I=K[D]L_1+⋯+K[D]L_n. Choose a nonzero L∈I having least possible order. The differential-operator ring admits division with remainder on the right: for every P∈K[D], one can successively cancel leading terms to write P=QL+R, where R=0 or ord(R)<ord(L). If P∈I, then R=P−QL also belongs to I. By the minimal choice of L, R must therefore be zero. Hence every P∈I is a left multiple of L, and consequently I=K[D]L. In particular, there are operators A_1,…,A_n and B_1,…,B_n such that

    L=Σ_{j=1}^n A_jL_j,                 L_j=B_jL  (1≤j≤n).

Define f=Σ_{j=1}^n A_j(f_j), and let

    ψ := ⋀_{j=1}^n (f_j=B_j(f)).

This condition is independent of x. If L_jx=f_j for every j, then

    Lx=Σ_j A_j(L_jx)=Σ_j A_j(f_j)=f.

Moreover, using L_j=B_jL,

    f_j=L_jx=B_j(Lx)=B_j(f),

so ψ holds. Conversely, if Lx=f and ψ holds, then for every j,

    L_jx=B_j(Lx)=B_j(f)=f_j.

This proves the desired equivalence. If every L_j is zero, take L=0, f=0, and ψ:=⋀_j(f_j=0); the same equivalence is immediate. Thus the equation result is valid, including the zero-operator case.

The suggested operation of merely adding equations is not an equivalence-preserving step. For example, over a field of characteristic different from 2, the system x=0 and x=1 is inconsistent, whereas its sum 2x=1 has a solution. The missing information is precisely the x-free compatibility condition ψ constructed above.

We now disprove the claimed reduction for linear inequations. Take K=Q with the trivial derivation and let x range over Q. With L_1=L_2=1, g_1=0, and g_2=1, the conjunction is

    x≠0 ∧ x≠1,

whose solution set is Q∖{0,1}. Suppose it were equivalent to Mx≠g ∧ ψ for some linear differential operator M∈Q[D] and some ψ containing neither x nor its derivatives. Once all parameters are fixed, ψ has a fixed truth value. Since Q∖{0,1} is nonempty, ψ would have to be true. Write M=Σ_{i=0}^r a_iD^i. Because the derivation on Q is trivial, D^i x=0 for every i≥1, so Mx=a_0x. If a_0=0, the inequation Mx≠g defines either all of Q or the empty set. If a_0≠0, it defines Q with the single point g/a_0 removed. Neither possibility equals Q∖{0,1}. This is a contradiction. Therefore a finite conjunction of linear differential inequations cannot in general be reduced to one linear differential inequation plus an x-free condition.

The slack-variable argument fails for the same reason: although Lx≠g can be expressed as Lx=g+b with b≠0, two nonzero residuals a and b may satisfy a+b=0, so adding the equalities does not yield a nonzero residual. Requiring a,b>0 is unavailable in an arbitrary differential field and, even over an ordered field, the original inequations do not imply that their residuals are positive.

There is a correct nonlinear replacement. Since a differential field has no zero divisors,

    ⋀_{j=1}^n (L_jx≠g_j)  ⇔  ∏_{j=1}^n (L_jx−g_j)≠0.

The expression on the right is one differential-polynomial inequation, but for n>1 it is generally nonlinear in x. If the resulting inequation is required to remain linear, the counterexample proves that no such general reduction exists.
